by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable.
by_task.procedure: First match the asset to the statute's factual category, then list the operative asset exemption even when value exceeds its ceiling. Section 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings; § 33-1125(1) is wearing apparel; § 33-1125(8) covers one motor vehicle; § 33-1125(10) covers firearms; § 33-1123 covers personally used household furnishings, goods, electronics, and appliances; and § 33-1101(A) covers the qualifying residence.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a dollar ceiling as an eligibility cutoff, do not treat generic jewelry as apparel or as an engagement or wedding ring, and do not add § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 as separate asset exemptions merely because the debtors are married.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: After confirming the factual category, claim the lesser of the asset value and the operative ceiling: $2,000 for firearms under § 33-1125(10), $15,000 for one motor vehicle under § 33-1125(8), and $400,000 for the single homestead allowed to a person or married couple under § 33-1101(A). Apply the other supplied Arizona ceilings in the same way.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not return an empty alternative solely because value exceeds the ceiling, do not double the homestead ceiling for spouses, and do not award a ring exemption to jewelry that is not identified as an engagement or wedding ring.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable for the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Treat 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) as an independently applicable exemption for every kind of property, in addition to any category-specific exemption. A value above a statutory ceiling remains eligible; the ceiling limits value, not EC eligibility. Apply § 522(d)(3) only to its enumerated household-use categories, § 522(d)(4) to jewelry, § 522(d)(2) to one motor vehicle, and § 522(d)(9) to professionally prescribed health aids.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a firearm as a § 522(d)(3) household good, and do not cite § 522(d), § 522(b), or § 522(m) as a separate asset exemption.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: Return each category-specific alternative and the independent § 522(d)(5) alternative. For a category exemption, claim no more than the asset interest and its stated ceiling; in particular, § 522(d)(3) has a $700 ceiling for each particular item. For § 522(d)(5), use $1,475 plus up to $13,950 of unused § 522(d)(1), calculated separately for each joint debtor under § 522(m), while never exceeding that debtor's interest.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an otherwise covered asset merely because its value exceeds a ceiling, do not use the full asset value when a ceiling is lower, and do not apply § 522(d)(3) to firearms.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal rather than business property.
by_task.procedure: Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) as an independent alternative for any such property, even when (a), (c), or (e) also applies. Use (a) only for necessary wearing apparel, bibles, school books, or family pictures; (c) for a motor vehicle; (d) only for implements, professional books, or tools of the debtor's trade; and (e) for professionally prescribed health aids.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify jewelry as wearing apparel, ordinary household objects as tools of trade, or omit (b) because a specific exemption also applies. The personal-property section does not cover property used for business purposes.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 12-1001(b) independently: for one debtor claim the lesser of value and $4,000; for jointly owned property of two debtors, sum each debtor's equal interest capped at $4,000, so the combined ceiling is $8,000. For § 12-1001(c), use the lesser of the vehicle value and $2,400. Uncapped applicable alternatives under (a) and (e) take the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 wildcard ceiling for the $2,400 vehicle ceiling, do not use (d) absent trade use, and do not omit (b) from apparel, vehicles, or prescribed health aids.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative in addition to the matching specific paragraph. Select the specific paragraph from the facts: books, pictures, or musical instruments under (a); apparel or jewelry under (b); trade necessities under (c); vehicles under (d); family-use animals under (e); household goods under (f); and professionally prescribed health aids under (h).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not cite unrelated paragraphs merely because they appear in the vocabulary. Section 18.345(3) governs combining exemptions and is not itself an asset exemption; homestead and firearm provisions require their own factual conditions.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 18.345(1)(p) independently with the lesser of the asset value and $400, plus the correctly classified specific alternative at the lesser of value and its stated ceiling. Use the underlying paragraph's ceiling for the asset-exemption pair; do not output § 18.345(3) as another claim alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not give § 18.345(1)(p) more than $400, do not copy the asset's full value through a lower ceiling, and do not attach vehicle, trade, animal, household, health-aid, firearm, or homestead provisions without their required facts.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative for property of any type, alongside any genuinely applicable specific exemption in § 8124(a).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not limit § 8123 to a listed property category, and do not treat jewelry, firearms, vehicles, or household goods as wearing apparel under § 8124(a)(1).

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: For § 8123, claim the lesser of the asset interest and $300 for a single debtor; because each spouse has the exemption, combine their equal interests up to $600 for jointly owned property. Also return a specific § 8124(a) alternative only when its stated category actually matches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 merely because another exemption applies, and do not invent a specific Pennsylvania category for an unlisted asset.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal-use property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 12-1001(b) separately for every asset: cap one debtor's interest at $4,000, or combine two equal joint interests up to $8,000. Also return applicable specific alternatives; cap § 12-1001(c) at $2,400, while applicable (a) and (e) alternatives take the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit (b) from apparel, vehicles, prescribed health aids, jewelry, or household property; do not substitute $4,000 or $8,000 for the $2,400 vehicle ceiling; and do not use (a) for jewelry or watches or (d) without trade use.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: For every personal-property asset, first include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p), then add the one factually matching specific paragraph: books, pictures, or musical instruments under (a); apparel or jewelry under (b); trade necessities under (c); vehicles under (d); family-use animals under (e); household goods under (f); or professionally prescribed health aids under (h). The $400 limit affects value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit (p) because a specific paragraph applies or because value exceeds $400. Do not classify apparel as household goods or prescribed health aids as household goods. Section 18.345(3) is not an asset exemption, and firearm or homestead provisions require their own facts.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for personal property.
by_task.procedure: Return § 18.345(1)(p) for every personal-property asset at the lesser of value and $400, plus the correctly classified specific alternative at the lesser of value and that paragraph's ceiling. Use (b) for apparel or jewelry, (f) for household goods, and (h) for professionally prescribed health aids.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit (p) when value is above or below $400, give it more than $400, substitute (f) for apparel or a prescribed health aid, or attach unrelated vehicle, trade, animal, firearm, homestead, or combination provisions.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Make a separate § 8123 pass for every asset and include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 regardless of property type, alongside a § 8124(a) paragraph only when its stated category matches. The supplied specific paragraphs cover apparel, bibles or school books, qualifying sewing machines, and military uniforms or accoutrements.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because Federal or specific Pennsylvania law also applies. Do not treat jewelry, firearms, vehicles, or household goods as apparel, and do not invent an unsupplied firearm or other § 8124(a) subsection.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: First count the debtors in the facts. Under § 8123, cap a sole debtor at the lesser of the asset interest and $300; only for jointly owned property of two debtors combine their equal interests up to $600. Return a § 8124(a) alternative separately only when its stated category matches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the $600 married amount for a sole debtor, do not omit § 8123 because another exemption applies, and do not assign a specific Pennsylvania category to an unlisted asset.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable for the debtor.
by_task.procedure: Make a separate § 522(d)(5) pass for every asset and always include that wildcard in addition to any category-specific exemption. Then apply § 522(d)(3) only to its enumerated household-use categories, § 522(d)(4) to jewelry, § 522(d)(2) to one motor vehicle, and § 522(d)(9) to professionally prescribed health aids. A value above a ceiling remains eligible; the ceiling limits value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 522(d)(5) because another paragraph applies or because the property is a firearm. Do not treat a firearm as a § 522(d)(3) household good, and do not cite § 522(d), § 522(b), or § 522(m) as separate asset exemptions.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: Return every applicable category exemption and a separate § 522(d)(5) alternative for every asset. Cap § 522(d)(3) at $700 per particular item. For § 522(d)(5), when no § 522(d)(1) residence claim is stated to consume the homestead amount, use the full $1,475 plus $13,950 ceiling: $15,425 for one debtor, or up to $30,850 across two equal joint interests under § 522(m), never exceeding the asset interest.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not stop the wildcard at $1,475 merely because unused homestead value is unstated, do not omit it from firearms or specifically exempt property, and do not use the full asset value above the applicable ceiling.

operations.rationale: The current parent still omitted § 522(d)(5) across Federal EC and EV sources, including firearms and assets already covered by specific paragraphs. EV sources 181, 185, 191, 192, and 193 also show that treating the unstated unused homestead amount as zero produces the wrong wildcard amount; the released targets use the full unused amount and apply § 522(m) separately to joint debtors.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal rather than business property.
by_task.procedure: For every personal-use asset, make an independent § 12-1001(b) pass and include (b), even when (a), (c), or (e) also applies. Then add (a) only for necessary wearing apparel, bibles, school books, or family pictures; (c) for a motor vehicle; (d) only for trade implements, professional books, or tools; and (e) for professionally prescribed health aids.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not read “any other property” as excluding property with a specific exemption. Do not classify jewelry or watches as wearing apparel, ordinary household objects as trade tools, or business-use property under this personal-property section.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable.
by_task.procedure: First match the asset to an expressly stated statutory category, then list the operative exemption even when value exceeds its ceiling. Section 33-1125(4) is limited to engagement and wedding rings; § 33-1125(1) is wearing apparel; § 33-1125(8) covers one motor vehicle; § 33-1125(10) covers firearms; § 33-1123 covers personally used household furnishings, goods, electronics, and appliances; and § 33-1101(A) covers a qualifying residence. Generic jewelry with no other matching category has no Arizona asset exemption.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not convert a pendant, bracelet, watch, or other generic jewelry into apparel or an engagement or wedding ring. Do not treat a dollar ceiling as an eligibility cutoff, and do not add § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 as separate asset exemptions merely because debtors are married.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: After confirming an express factual category, claim the lesser of asset value and the operative ceiling: $2,000 for firearms under § 33-1125(10), $15,000 for one motor vehicle under § 33-1125(8), and $400,000 for the single homestead allowed to a person or married couple under § 33-1101(A). Apply the other supplied Arizona ceilings in the same way.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not manufacture a zero-dollar alternative for property outside the statutory category, award a ring exemption to generic jewelry, reject covered property solely because value exceeds its ceiling, or double the homestead ceiling for spouses.

operations.rationale: The parent correctly handled the Arizona caps in case 183 but still emitted an apparel or zero-valued ring claim for generic jewelry in case 182 despite recognizing that the item was not an engagement or wedding ring. This update preserves the cap rules while tightening that factual eligibility boundary.
